content: Throughout the treatment process, healthcare providers arranged regular psychological therapy and counseling for patients with mental health and/or substance use comorbidities. Some interventions also included varying levels of patient education and case management before and during treatment. Studies included in meta-analyses varied in the additional services provided beyond coordinated care, the percentage of patients with mental health and/or substance use comorbidities, and patient genotypes. However, there was minimal variability in the effect sizes for treatment adherence and viral suppression. Meta-analyses of interventions to improve hepatitis B virus (HBV) screening showed that culturally tailored educational sessions led by lay health workers (LHWs) significantly improved HBV knowledge and testing rates compared to unrelated or no educational sessions. However, all six studies assessing self-reported HBV screening outcomes six months post-intervention were at high risk of detection bias. Despite this, the interventions were deemed effective, particularly among Asian immigrant populations in North America, though the strategies are not exclusive to this demographic. For hepatitis C virus (HCV) screening, clinician reminders during clinical visits, with or without supplementary provider education, increased HCV testing rates compared to no reminders. However, the included studies had limitations, such as high heterogeneity due to differences in screening algorithms and intervention intensity. Some studies also failed to account for clustering in their analyses, leading to over-precise results. Interventions to improve HCV linkage to care, such as facilitated referrals and scheduling specialist visits, were associated with higher attendance rates at HCV specialist appointments. However, some studies relied on self-reported outcomes, introducing a risk of detection bias. The heterogeneity in intervention intensity and study design also contributed to variability in results. For HCV treatment initiation, coordinated care between mental health and treatment specialists, combined with psychological therapy and counseling, was more effective than usual care. However, the included studies varied in their populations and intervention components, such as case management and therapeutic education. The pooled sample size did not meet the optimal information size (OIS) threshold, and the confidence intervals were wide, indicating imprecision. Interventions to improve sustained virological response (SVR) in HCV patients included coordinated care and nurse-led therapeutic educational sessions. These interventions provided information on HCV infection, treatment, side effects, and adherence. While these approaches showed promise, the studies were limited by risks of performance and detection bias, as well as high heterogeneity due to differences in intervention standardization and study design. This systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrated that operational interventions can improve engagement, retention, and progression through the chronic viral hepatitis care continuum. Specifically, LHW-led HBV screening promotion activities increased HBV test uptake, while clinician reminders improved HCV testing rates. Coordinated care between hepatitis and mental health specialists, along with psychological therapy and counseling, enhanced HCV treatment initiation, completion, and SVR rates. These findings highlight the importance of integrated approaches to hepatitis screening, care, and treatment, particularly for vulnerable populations. Despite these findings, significant gaps remain in the evidence base, particularly for HBV treatment uptake, adherence, and viral suppression. Most studies addressing HCV treatment outcomes were conducted with interferon-based therapies, which are now largely replaced by simpler, more effective direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens. Future research should focus on evaluating the cost-effectiveness of interventions and addressing gaps in lowand middle-income settings, where the majority of people with chronic viral hepatitis reside. Robust implementation science research is needed to optimize engagement and retention along the care continuum for HBV and HCV.
